title: Game-Theoretic Co-Evolution for LLM-Based Heuristic Discovery
one_liner: Instead of testing a discovered solver on a fixed pile of cases, the paper lets a solver and a case generator keep improving against each other so the solver learns under pressure from harder cases.
lead: Automatic heuristic discovery asks a language model to write small solver programs for hard search or planning tasks. The usual training loop scores those programs on a fixed set of cases. That is easy to run, but it teaches the solver to fit yesterday's test set instead of learning rules that still work when the cases shift. This paper replaces the fixed test set with a live opponent: one side searches for better solver programs, while the other side searches for harder cases. Because each side keeps responding to the other, the solver is trained on cases that expose its current weaknesses instead of cases chosen once at the start.

problem.h2: Fixed evaluation teaches the wrong lesson
paras: Suppose you ask a system to invent a search rule for a combinatorial problem such as packing, routing, or scheduling. You need a way to score each candidate rule. The common choice is simple: keep a fixed benchmark set of problem instances and reward any rule that solves those instances well.

That setup breaks once the solver starts adapting to the quirks of the fixed set. A candidate rule can look strong because it learned shortcuts that fit the benchmark rather than the real problem family. When the test cases change, those shortcuts fail because the rule never had to face an adversary that searched for its weak spots.

callout.html: A fixed case set rewards solvers that fit the benchmark, even when they fail on new cases, because the benchmark never fights back.

paras: The paper changes the evaluation loop around heuristic discovery. Instead of scoring solvers on a frozen case set, it turns evaluation into a two-player game between solver programs and instance-generator programs. The learned object is no longer one isolated heuristic; it is a solver that has survived repeated attack from generators chosen to expose its weaknesses.
object.object: mixed pools of solver programs and instance generators

hidden.name: expected score against the opponent mixture
paras: The important hidden quantity is not a solver's score on one benchmark. It is the solver's expected score against the current mixture of generators, together with a generator's expected damage against the current mixture of solvers. This tells you whether a new program is strong against the whole active ecosystem rather than one handpicked opponent.

That quantity matters because a best response to a mixture is harder to overfit. A solver that beats many generators in expectation usually learned broader decision rules, because it had to do well across several ways the task can become difficult. A generator that hurts many solvers in expectation usually found a real weakness pattern, because that pattern shows up across the pool rather than against one unlucky solver.

heat.caption: Darker means a stronger interaction under the current solver-generator game; bordered cells mark the high-pressure matchups that shape the next best responses.

reads.html: Do not ask only, 'Did this solver beat this one case set?' Ask, 'How well does this solver hold up against the whole active mix of hard case makers?'
The game value is the expected solver payoff under mixed meta-strategies on both sides. Best-response search expands the solver pool and the generator pool by targeting this expectation directly.

paras: A fixed case set goes stale. Once a solver learns its patterns, progress on the benchmark no longer means progress on the underlying problem. Co-evolution avoids this because the generator keeps searching for cases where the solver still fails. Every time the solver improves, the generator must search for a new weakness because the old one may no longer work.

The solver side benefits because the weighted mix of cases becomes an adaptive curriculum. Early on, the generator finds obvious weaknesses, so the solver learns basic competence. Later, easy exploits disappear, so the generator is forced to search for subtler weaknesses. This stages the learning process automatically because pressure rises with solver ability.

The generator side also matters. If you optimize only the solver, you may never discover rare but important failure modes. By optimizing generators against a mixture of solvers, the method keeps producing cases that stay informative for more than one solver. That is why the paper reports better out-of-distribution behavior: the solver was trained under a changing adversary rather than a frozen teacher.

stages.s: Current pool of solver programs and current pool of case generators
Compute mixed payoffs across solver-generator pairs
Ask the language model for a solver best response to the mixed generators
Ask the language model for a generator best response to the mixed solvers
Expanded pools and a harder training game

math.words: Take every solver in the pool and every generator in the pool. Weight each pair by how often the current mixed strategy uses that solver and that generator. Then add the solver's payoff on that pair. The result is the solver's expected value against the live opponent mixture.
math.equation: V(p, q) = sum_i sum_j p_i * q_j * u(solver_i, generator_j)
symbols: expected solver payoff under solver mixture p and generator mixture q
probability of choosing solver i from the solver pool
probability of choosing generator j from the generator pool
payoff when solver i is tested on cases produced by generator j
add the contribution from every solver-generator pair

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the solver pool has two programs: S1 and S2. The generator pool has two programs: G1 and G2.
Current solver mixture: p = [0.6, 0.4]. Current generator mixture: q = [0.5, 0.5].
A new solver is useful only if it raises this mixed value, because that means it beats the active range of hard cases instead of one narrow slice.

math.note: The paper keeps expanding the pools because a strong best response changes the mixture value for everyone else, which creates the next opening for improvement.

bars.h2: Why the adaptive game beats static testing

charts.title: Static benchmark training
charts.note: The solver can look strong on the fixed benchmark because the benchmark stops changing, so hidden weaknesses remain untested.

charts.title: ASRO co-evolution
charts.note: The score stays high on shifted cases because the solver trained against generators that kept searching for failures instead of repeating the same old cases.

items.html: If the language model cannot produce strong new solver or generator programs, the pools stop improving. The game then becomes shallow because both sides repeat small variations instead of finding new pressure points.

If the payoff rewards only one narrow metric, the solver may learn bad behavior that still scores well. This matters because the generator will then attack the wrong objective too, so the whole game drifts away from the real task.
If one generator dominates too early, the solver may overfit to that one style of hard case again. Keeping a mixture matters because diversity is what forces broad solver behavior.

Use payoffs that reflect the real optimization target, maintain diverse pools on both sides, and keep adding strong best responses. Then each new round stays informative because one side's gain exposes the other side's next weakness.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny bin-packing or routing task. Let one program propose a heuristic solver and another program propose hard instances. Keep a pool of both. In each round, estimate mixed payoffs, ask the writer model for one new solver and one new instance generator, and add them only if they improve the mixture value because that means they helped against the active opponent pool rather than a single easy case. Track performance on both a fixed validation set and a held-out shifted set.
demo.closing: The demo should show that the co-evolved solver does better on shifted cases because the generator kept finding failures during training, so the solver had to learn broader rules instead of memorizing one frozen benchmark.
